h1: Naming a beer that works in more than one language
title: Naming a Beer for Many Languages | Craft Beer School
desc: How to test a beer name across languages before you print labels: meaning, sound, script and the checks that avoid expensive mistakes.
teaser: A name that sounds great at home can mean something awkward elsewhere. Test it before the labels are printed.
standfirst: A beer name is a small thing that travels a long way. This guide gives a process for testing a name in the languages where it will be sold.
sections:
Names fail in a few predictable ways. The word means something unfortunate in another language. It is hard to pronounce. It sounds like a rude or unrelated word. Or it is simply already used by someone else in that market.

None of these are rare. They happen because the name was chosen at a kitchen table by people who speak one language. The fix is a short, dull process done before the design agency starts.

A dictionary check is a start, not an answer. Slang, regional words and brand names all carry meanings that a dictionary misses. Ask native speakers from the country you plan to sell in, not only from the language in general. Portuguese in Brazil and Portugal, or Spanish in Mexico and Spain, can differ sharply.

Ask three questions. What does it mean? What does it remind you of? Would you be happy to order it out loud? The third question catches the names that read fine but sound awkward at a bar.

Say the name aloud with someone who does not know it. If they hesitate, a customer will hesitate too. Watch for sounds that do not exist in the target language. Names with double consonants, clusters or accents may be mangled by menus, search engines and point-of-sale systems that cannot print the characters.

Consider the script. A name in the Latin alphabet may look foreign and be unreadable where another script dominates. Some brewers add a second line in the local script. Hire a native-speaking designer to write it, because a poorly drawn version looks worse than none.

A name that clears the language test may still be taken. Search trademark registers and the open web for the name in your target markets before you fall in love with it. Registration is territorial. A mark that is free in one country may be owned in the next. Protecting a beer name in more than one country covers the process.

Do not treat a quick online search as clearance. Use a trademark attorney for the final check. This guide is general guidance, not legal advice.

Many countries limit what a label may say about style, origin or strength. Terms that are fine in one place can be restricted in another. Place-names and style terms in particular may be protected. Read the label rules for each market. See what a beer label must show.

If your name refers to a place, a saint, a flag or a national symbol, check local rules and sensitivities. Local advisers are cheaper than a recall.
Beer names versus the brand name

A brewery usually has one brand name and many beer names. The brand name needs the hardest testing because it sits on everything. Individual beer names can change with the season or the market, which gives you room to localise. Keep a tidy sheet that lists every name, the markets where it is cleared and the markets where it is not.

Some brewers use numbers or style names for the beers and keep the brand name as the one thing that must travel. That removes a lot of risk, though it also removes a little personality. Decide which trade you prefer.

Once the finalist has passed the language checks, put it on a mock-up can or tap handle and show it to people in the target market. Ask them to describe the beer they expect from the name. If their picture is a dark stout and you brew a pale lager, the name is sending the wrong message.

Record their first reactions before you explain anything. The first five seconds are the only honest ones.

1. Shortlist five names, not one.
  2. Run meaning and sound tests with native speakers in each target market.
  3. Search registers and the web.
  4. Check how the name looks in the local script, if different.
  5. Ask a trademark attorney to clear the finalist.
  6. Test it on a cheap label mock-up with ten real drinkers.

Naming is a discipline with a method. A short course on naming and trademarks for drinks brands teaches that method with examples, so your finalist survives the checks.
faqs: Should I use one name everywhere?
A single name is simpler and cheaper to protect. If it fails in a market, a local variant may be safer. Test before deciding.
Is a Google search enough to check a name?
No. It misses trademark registers and local words. Ask a trademark attorney for clearance.
Can a name be too descriptive?
Yes. Descriptive names are often harder to protect. Rules vary by country.
Do I need the name in a local script?
Only if you sell where another script dominates. Have a native speaker create it.
